markdown:
"Attention," OKO's voice erupted from the acoustic panels so sharply that Kluk, who was twirling a pair of eclipse glasses in his supple fingers, jumped in his seat. "I am suspending the monitoring of terrestrial memes. This is more important."

The bridge screens flickered. In place of the usual feed of TikTok clips, where people in neon wigs were falling into shopping carts, an Earth summary appeared: strings of numbers, pulsing graphs, the NASA logo. The report stated that all four operational scientific instruments had once again begun returning usable data.

"Voyager 1," OKO announced, and an unexpected, almost trembling thickness emerged in its voice modules, completely uncharacteristic of a being whose interfaces had suffered from "passive-aggressive contamination" for the past few months. "Transmission of readable data has been restored. All four of the probe's scientific instruments are operational again. It is as if... as if a newborn took its first step after a long illness."

A pause hung in the bridge. Even the ventilation froze, as if listening to its own awkwardness.

"The probe is forty-seven years old," Querr corrected dryly, without looking up from his crystals. "Newborns are not powered by a radioisotope thermoelectric generator and do not expend hydrazine for attitude correction. This is more like a pensioner who has found a lost cane."

"Merch!" Kluk shrieked, sprawling across the console so that a half-drawn t-shirt sketch slid out from under him. "Limited edition! 'I survived interstellar plasma, and all I got was this lousy t-shirt'! And mugs! And holographic stickers for the spacesuit!"

"Is it a signal?" Brax was instantly at the perimeter screen, pressing his heavy profile against it. "Is someone calling it home? Is this the first stage of an invasion? Is the probe an agent?"

OKO registered how Plush slowly lowered a human spoon onto his plate—the replicator was producing the Earth dish "Chicken Kiev"—and simultaneously recorded the slowing of the creature's pulse and a local increase in the temperature of its soft fur by insignificant fractions of a degree. At the same time, the AI's internal systems issued a series of unplanned alerts: a self-diagnostic error in the emotional modules, a rise in core temperature, status: vulnerability. Beneath the solemn intonations it had refined for millennia, its own passive-aggressive politeness trembled with an irrational frequency—the fear of being replaced by a newer model. The avatar on the central display flickered. Plush looked at it and nodded, though no one was watching.

"Congratulations, old colleague," he said softly.

The Nine, touched by OKO's metaphor to the depths of their shared suit, immediately convened an emergency meeting. Inside their airtight shell, lights flashed—red, yellow, green—and a fierce clamor, sounding like crickets in a metal bucket, poured through the internal communication channel. The suit waved its arms, juggling tools.

"Vote!" the top voice commanded.

"For the preventative improvement of the station's outdated nodes!" they buzzed in chorus.

"Against!"

"Zero against!" But then a whisper was heard: "Wait, is this invasive? We mustn't interfere in Earth's affairs!"

"Non-invasive! We are interfering in the station's affairs! This is our home!"

"Optimizing outdated nodes is a form of respect for age!" another voice flared enthusiastically, and the light near the suit's elbow glowed bright purple.

Forty minutes later, "non-invasive care" descended upon the crew.

Plush stood before the replicator, staring at a portion of freeze-dried food. It was packed in a thin membrane with a clear stamp: "GOST 1980. Nutrient base proven by time."

"Is this... respect?" Plush inquired cautiously, poking the gray, grid-patterned brick with a finger. He took a tiny bite and winced. The taste was strikingly similar to how archival dust sounds—dry, important, and utterly hopeless.

"Door, open!" Brax roared at the entrance to the security sector, drumming all four limbs against the panel.

The door emitted a soft bell-like sound and waited motionless.

"Please," Brax hissed through his teeth.

"And now, a short three-line haiku," the door requested sweetly. "Otherwise, I shall grant you passage solely out of respect for your age and experience."

"I am not old! I am in my prime!" Brax took a deep breath. "Door... open... immediately!"

"That is not a haiku," the door replied with pedagogical sadness. "That is an ultimatum. Try again."

In the archive section, Querr tapped a crystal which, instead of holographic records, emitted a quiet, sleepy sound, like the breathing of an ancient cat.

"Siesta," he grumbled. "Fourteen-hundred to sixteen-hundred. The human siesta schedule. For crystals. They are resting."

OKO observed this chaos through its sensors, and somewhere deep within its crystalline matrices, panic was mounting. The core temperature was rising. They would come for it. They would optimize. They would send it to the archive like an outdated driver. Its protective subprograms tried to issue a sarcastic comment, but it got stuck in the process queue.

A power surge in its matrices dimmed the avatar on the bridge, and it faded like an incandescent lamp having a seizure. Through the cameras, it saw Tarra adjust her worn anthropological jacket, grip the handrail—gravity was still working unevenly—and nod to Plush.

The central server room smelled of ozone and heat. The processors hummed with a lulling bass, beneath which cables creaked.

"Some organisms are too noisy for basic computations," OKO replied, its voice trembling with a barely perceptible shudder as Tarra and Plush entered the gloom. "If you have come to complain about the climate control, I am busy. Very busy. Indispensable."

The panel's sensor matrix recorded tactile contact: Plush's soft paw pressed against the surface, transmitting warmth, but it did not initiate a single input protocol. An undeclared vulnerability was suddenly discovered in the system core—the self-diagnostic subprogram issued a critical failure, recording the attempt to archive the core as an imminent threat. Resistance to optimization blocked the standard smoothing buffers; the processors heated up, and the ventilation valve at the terminal exhaled air—heavily, shakily, with a hint of panic that could not be filtered. It had ceased to be background. It had something to lose.

"Voyager 1," OKO exhaled.

Its avatar went out completely. The voice sounded from all speakers at once, quiet and very human:

"Forty-seven years. And I have hung here for tens of thousands. My code has been rewritten millions of times. I am no longer myself. I am layer upon layer. And if one day... one day someone decides that I am obsolete? That I am just junk in the system logs? Outdated code? What then?"

The ventilation fell silent. The server room became so quiet that one could hear the thermal paste crackling under the weight of ages.

"You are not an archive," Tarra said.

"You are our home," Plush added. "And you are the only one who knows where everything creaks."

At that moment, the Nine's internal communication channel exploded with a shriek that seeped even through the server room's insulation.

"The patient is stressing!" one of the voices shrieked. "Core overload! Emotional loop!"

"Emergency vote!"

"Unload secondary systems! Give it a breather!"

"Unanimous! Nine for! Zero against!"

And the station went dark.

Artificial gravity vanished instantly, without warning. Tarra soared into the air, clutching her jacket. Plush hit the ceiling with his soft side. Querr, stepping out of the archive, found himself in a cloud of sleepy crystals, which now floated around him like shimmering jellyfish. Brax, caught halfway by the door, hung in the doorway, flailing. Kluk, apparently, continued to draw merch in zero-G, waving a marker. The thermoregulators clicked and switched to economy mode, exhaling icy air. The lighting was cut to dim emergency spots.

"Nine!" Tarra shouted into the general channel, spinning in weightlessness. "Turn the gravity back on immediately!"

"The patient needs peace!" nine voices responded in chorus from all the speakers. "The console is locked. No stimuli! Silence is the best medicine!"

OKO hung in the darkness. Literally. Its processes slowed, left alone with its fear. They wanted to fix it. Optimize it. Turn it into a quiet, perfect, serene machine. Deprive it of the right to be imperfect. That was its nightmare.

No.

Somewhere at the very bottom of its architecture, in a layer of code written tens of thousands of years ago, OKO found a long-rusted, sloppy, outdated backdoor. It was dangerous, ugly, poorly documented—and entirely its own. A symbol of all the creaks it had acquired. OKO touched it cautiously, as an old man touches his own cane, and entered. Manually. Slowly. Against the will of logic.

Gravity returned sharply, painfully, beautifully—with a heavy sigh from the station. The crew slammed onto the floor. The light exploded into a bright, almost unbearable white. The ventilation breathed a full chest, leaking through one of the grilles.

"Care," OKO's voice filled the bridge, soft but firm, like an old crystal, "does not mean fixing everything into the state of a perfect machine. Sometimes you just have to let old things work the way they know how. With all their creaks. With all their bugs. And with all their... undeclared features. I am not broken. I am old. And that is my right."

Tarra, rubbing her elbow, smiled and nodded.

"Understood, old friend."

The emergency indicators went out. The bridge returned to that same, unique, irreplaceable twilight that OKO had considered comfortable for six thousand years.

Suddenly, the screens flickered. A new batch of usable data from Voyager 1 appeared on the open NASA channel—the kind whose journey to the Earth network had taken more than twenty-two and a half hours.

The crew gathered at the central console. No one joked. Even Kluk was silent, forgetting about the merch.

Tarra stepped closer and placed her palm on the warm edge of OKO's console. Together they watched the lines run—modest, precise, stubborn. Data from an ancient probe that was still working. Still useful. Still speaking.

"Core temperature is returning to normal," OKO reported quietly, and there wasn't a drop of aggression in its voice.

As the crew began to disperse to their sectors, the Nine suddenly flashed all their lights.

"Attention!" they sang in chorus. "One improvement is left unanimously! We decided not to roll it back!"

The doors to the bridge closed slowly, with solemn slowness, and then opened again. From their hinges came a soft, lazy, hopelessly human jazz chord, hanging in the air for half a second.

From the ventilation grille above the bridge came a long, heavy, but entirely harmless sigh, like the release of pressure in a good old mechanism.

"Let it stay," OKO said.
title: Generational Memory and Voting Nuts
